desc:
The array nums has length n and every element lies in the range 1..n. Each value occurs either once or twice. Return all values that occur twice, in ascending order (an empty array if there are none).

Aim for O(n) time and no extra data structure beyond the output (you may use the input array itself as scratch space).

Example: nums = [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1] returns [2, 3].
constraints: Each value occurs at most twice
hints: A count map is the obvious tool. To save the memory, ask where you could store one bit of information per value 1..n.
Value v can be associated with index v - 1. Because all values are positive, the sign of nums[v - 1] is a free bit.
For each element take v = abs(x). If nums[v - 1] is already negative, you have seen v before, so it is a repeat; otherwise negate it. Sort the collected repeats at the end.
editorial: Because the values are exactly the valid indices shifted by one, the array can double as a visited table. Walk through the array; for every element look at v = abs(nums[i]). If nums[v - 1] is positive, flip it to negative to record that v has been seen. If it is already negative, v was seen earlier, so v is a repeated value.

Reading the absolute value is important because earlier steps may already have negated the current element. Each value occurs at most twice, so each repeat is reported exactly once. The repeats are discovered in an arbitrary order, so sort them at the end, which costs O(k log k) for k repeats (k is at most n/2).
A hash set is simpler and equally O(n) in time but uses O(n) extra space.
time: O(n + k log k) for k repeats
